mots.sens: The word 'prophet' refers to a spokesperson for God, someone who speaks on behalf of God. In the Old Testament, prophets were often called to convey messages of rebuke, comfort, or promise. Their role was crucial in guiding God's people and reminding them of His ways. Theologically, this underscores the importance of divine revelation and communication between God and humanity.

The term 'many' indicates the diversity and multiplicity of ways in which God has communicated with His people. This reflects the richness of divine revelation throughout history, using various means such as visions, dreams, and oracles. Spiritually, it reminds us that God is active and eager to make Himself known, adapting to our human understanding.

The word 'time' in this context evokes a specific moment in the history of divine revelation. It emphasizes that God has chosen specific moments to speak to His people, reminding us that His word is always relevant and timely. This encourages us to be attentive to the moments when God may speak to us today.

1.epoque: The book of Hebrews was written in a context of persecution and questioning of the Christian faith, probably between 60 and 70 A.D.
1.passage: This verse introduces the idea that God spoke to humanity through the prophets before fully revealing His will through Jesus Christ, thus establishing the superiority of Christian revelation.
1.culture: In Jewish culture, prophets were central figures, and their message was often linked to the law and the promises of God. This shows the importance of continuity between the Old and New Testaments.
1.interpretation: This verse highlights the transition of God's revelation, moving from the prophets to Jesus, the Son. It shows that Jesus is the culmination of divine communication, and that all previous promises and revelations find their fulfillment in Him.
1.commentaire: This passage reminds us that God desires to communicate with us and has used many means to do so. As believers, we must be attentive to His word and to the ways He reveals Himself in our lives today. This encourages us to seek a personal relationship with God, who still speaks through His Word and His Spirit.

mots.sens: The word 'Huios' means 'son' and evokes a relationship of authority and closeness. In the biblical context, it is often used to refer not only to a biological descendant but also to a unique spiritual relationship, such as that between God the Father and Jesus Christ. This underscores the divinity of Christ and His central role in the plan of salvation, affirming that He is the heir of all things.

This term means 'heir' and implies the possession and transmission of goods or rights. In the context of this verse, it emphasizes that Christ is the heir of all created things, which grants Him supreme authority over the universe. This reinforces the idea that everything that exists belongs to Christ, and that through Him, we have access to this inheritance.

The word 'Kosmos' refers to the universe, to the order of the created world. It implies not only physical creation but also the idea of a divine order established by God. In this verse, it emphasizes that Christ is not only the creator but also has authority over all of creation, which is fundamental to understanding His role in salvation.

This term means 'has spoken' and indicates divine communication. In the context of this verse, it emphasizes that God has chosen to reveal Himself to humanity through His Son, Jesus Christ. This highlights the importance of divine revelation and the necessity to listen to and respond to this word.

2.epoque: The book of Hebrews was written in a context of persecution and uncertainty for early Christians, probably between 60 and 70 A.D.
2.passage: This passage is at the beginning of the letter to the Hebrews, which establishes the superiority of Christ over the prophets and angels, affirming His unique role in God's plan.
2.culture: In the Jewish culture of the time, the concept of inheritance was central, and the idea that the Messiah would be the heir of all things resonated deeply with messianic expectations.
2.interpretation: This verse emphasizes that God has chosen to fully reveal Himself through His Son, Jesus Christ, who is both creator and heir. This reminds us that our understanding of God is mediated by the person of Christ, and that our relationship with Him is essential for our faith.
2.commentaire: This passage calls us to recognize the sovereignty of Christ over all creation and to listen to His voice. As Christians, we are called to live as heirs with Him, which gives us identity and mission. In meditating on this truth, we must commit to living according to His word and sharing this revelation with the world.

mots.sens: This term means 'reflection' or 'radiance', evoking the idea of light emanating from a source. It emphasizes that Jesus is the perfect manifestation of God's glory, thus revealing the divine nature to the world. In this verse, it indicates that seeing Jesus is seeing the glory of God, reinforcing the idea of incarnation and divine revelation.

This word translates to 'imprint' or 'character', and it designates the impression left by a seal. This means that Jesus is the exact expression of God's nature, bearing in Himself the fullness of divinity. Theologically, this reinforces the idea that Jesus is not just a messenger, but that He is Himself fully God.

This verb means 'to sit', and in this context, it evokes the idea of taking a position of authority and sovereignty. Jesus, sitting at the right hand of God, affirms His preeminence and power over all things. It also underscores the completion of His redemptive work, where He is exalted after having purified sins.

This term means 'purification', and it refers to the act of making pure or cleansing. In the context of this verse, it indicates that Jesus has accomplished the ultimate sacrifice for our sins, thus allowing reconciliation with God. Spiritually, this underscores the importance of grace and forgiveness offered by Christ.

3.epoque: The book of Hebrews was written in a context of persecution of Christians, probably between 60 and 70 A.D., as believers struggled to remain faithful in their faith amid external pressures.
3.passage: This passage is at the beginning of the letter to the Hebrews, which seeks to establish the superiority of Christ over angels, prophets, and the old system of the law. The author introduces here the divine nature of Jesus, emphasizing His central role in the plan of redemption.
3.culture: In the Jewish culture of the time, the understanding of God's glory was deeply rooted in history and sacred writings. The contrast between God's revelation in the Old Testament and the perfect revelation in Christ is a key understanding for Jewish readers.
3.interpretation: This verse reveals that Jesus is both fully God and fully man, uniting the two natures in one person. His position at the right hand of God symbolizes His supreme authority and His role as mediator between God and humanity, thus offering hope and assurance to believers.
3.commentaire: Hebrews 1:3 reminds us that Jesus is the perfect reflection of God's glory, and that in Him, we find the purification of our sins. This encourages us to approach Him with confidence, knowing that He is our Sovereign and our Savior. In meditating on this truth, we are called to live in the light of His grace and to testify to His glory in our daily lives.

mots.sens: This word means 'name' and goes beyond mere designation. In Jewish culture, a name is often associated with a person's identity, character, and authority. In this context, the 'name' that Christ has inherited emphasizes His superiority and divine authority, marking a clear distinction between Him and the angels, who are creatures. This reinforces the idea that Jesus is not only a messenger but the Son of God, possessing a divine nature and a unique mission.

This term means 'angel' and refers to celestial messengers. Angels are often perceived as powerful beings, servants of God, but here, the text highlights their inferior position compared to Christ. This reminds us that, although they have an important role in the divine plan, they cannot equal the majesty and authority of the Son, who has inherited a name that grants Him eternal superiority.

This word means 'superior' and indicates preeminence or excellence. It is used to describe Christ's position in relation to the angels, affirming that He is not only superior in quality but also in dignity. This superiority is essential for understanding the nature of Jesus as the Son of God, who is above all celestial powers.

4.epoque: The book of Hebrews was written in a context where Jewish Christians faced persecution and doubts about Christ's superiority over the law and Jewish traditions.
4.passage: This verse is part of an introduction that establishes Christ's superiority over the angels, a central theme of chapter 1, which underscores His divine nature and unique role as the Son of God.
4.culture: In Jewish culture, angels were revered as messengers of God, but the text questions this veneration by asserting that Jesus, as the Son, possesses an authority and name that surpass those of the angels.
4.interpretation: This verse reminds us that Jesus is not merely an angel or a messenger, but that He is the Son of God, having inherited a name that testifies to His divinity and authority. This encourages us to recognize the greatness of Christ in our faith and worship.
4.commentaire: This passage invites us to reflect on the majesty of Christ and our relationship with Him. By acknowledging His superiority, we are called to give Him a central place in our lives. This encourages us to live in accordance with His will, knowing that He has all power over heaven and earth.

mots.sens: This term means 'son' and evokes a relationship of intimacy and filiation. In the biblical context, it emphasizes not only physical descent but also a spiritual and authoritative relationship. By saying 'You are my Son,' God establishes a unique and eternal relationship with Jesus, who is both fully divine and fully human, thus affirming Christ's preeminence over all creatures, including angels.

This verb means 'to beget' and is used to describe the act of giving birth. In this verse, it emphasizes the idea of a divine generation, affirming that Jesus is not a created being but the eternal Son of God. This has profound implications for our understanding of the Trinity and the nature of Christ, affirming His authority and divinity.

This term means 'father' and represents a figure of authority, protection, and relationship. In the context of this verse, it emphasizes the intimate relationship between God the Father and Jesus the Son. This reinforces the understanding of God's nature as both transcendent and immanent, involved in the lives of His children.

5.epoque: This passage was written in a context where early Christians sought to understand the nature of Christ in light of the influence of Greek philosophies and Jewish teachings about angels and the Messiah.
5.passage: Hebrews chapter 1 establishes Christ's superiority over the angels, affirming His divinity and unique role as the Son of God. This verse cites passages from the Old Testament to demonstrate that Jesus is not an angel, but the beloved Son of God.
5.culture: In Jewish culture, the concept of divine sonship was very important, as it implied a covenant relationship. Angels were seen as messengers and servants, but here, the author of Hebrews emphasizes that Jesus holds a much higher position.
5.interpretation: This verse highlights the uniqueness of Jesus as the Son of God, distinguishing Him from the angels. It reminds us that our relationship with God is based on the spiritual sonship we have in Christ, which allows us to call God our Father.
5.commentaire: This passage invites us to recognize the greatness of Christ and to understand our identity as children of God. By accepting Jesus as our Savior, we enter into an intimate relationship with the Father, which transforms our daily lives. Let us reflect on the depth of this relationship and how it influences our way of living and witnessing our faith.

mots.sens: This term means 'firstborn' and denotes not only the order of birth but also a position of preeminence and honor. In the biblical context, it is often associated with Christ's primacy over all creation, highlighting His divine authority. Theologically, this reinforces the idea that Jesus is the Son of God, having a unique place in the plan of salvation.

This word refers to 'angels,' spiritual beings created by God to serve and worship. In the Bible, angels play a role as intermediaries between God and humanity, and their worship of Christ underscores the majesty and divinity of Jesus. Spiritually, this reminds us that even celestial powers recognize the sovereignty of the Son.

This verb means 'to worship' and implies an act of submission and reverence. In the context of this verse, it indicates that the worship of angels towards Christ is a recognition of His divinity and authority. This teaches us the importance of authentic worship in our relationship with God.

6.epoque: This passage was written in a context where early Christians struggled to understand the nature of Christ in light of Jewish and Greek influences of the time. The author of the epistle to the Hebrews seeks to establish Christ's superiority over the angels and ancient traditions.
6.passage: In this chapter, the author emphasizes Jesus' unique position as the Son of God by comparing Him to the angels. Verse 6 refers to a divine declaration that calls for the worship of Christ, reinforcing His divine status.
6.culture: In Jewish culture, the worship of angels was common, but here, the author shows that even these spiritual beings must worship Christ, which was a revolutionary concept for Jewish readers.
6.interpretation: This verse reminds us that Jesus, as the firstborn, is above all creatures, including angels. The instruction to worship the Son underscores the importance of recognizing Christ's divinity and our own position as worshipers before Him.
6.commentaire: This passage calls us to authentic worship of Christ, recognizing His supremacy over all things. As believers, we must remember that our worship should not be reserved for rituals, but should be an act of the heart, in response to the greatness of our Savior.

mots.sens: The term 'ἄγγελοι' translates to 'angels' and refers to divine messengers. In biblical tradition, angels are often perceived as spiritual beings sent by God to fulfill His will. Their primary function is to serve and convey messages, which emphasizes their role as intermediaries between God and humanity, thereby reinforcing the idea of divine sovereignty.

The word 'πνεῦμα' means 'wind' or 'spirit,' and evokes an invisible yet powerful force. In the biblical context, it can refer to the Spirit of God or spiritual forces. The use of this term here highlights the dynamic and active nature of angels, who, like the wind, are at God's service and act according to His will.

The word 'πῦρ' means 'fire' and often symbolizes purification, power, and divine presence in the Scriptures. In this verse, it evokes the fiery and purifying nature of God's servants, who are both powerful and protective. It also recalls the fire of God's presence, as seen in the Old Testament, where fire represents holiness and divine glory.

7.epoque: The book of Hebrews was written in a context where early Christians faced persecution and doubts regarding their faith, seeking to understand the superiority of Christ over the old Jewish traditions.
7.passage: In this passage, the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews makes a comparison between the Son of God and the angels, emphasizing that although they are powerful, angels are merely creatures serving the divine plan, while the Son is superior.
7.culture: The Jewish culture of the time valued angels as important figures in divine communication, but the author of the epistle reminds that their role is subordinate to that of Christ, who is the true mediator between God and humanity.
7.interpretation: This verse highlights the servant nature of angels while affirming the majesty and preeminence of Christ. It reminds us that although angels are powerful, their function is to serve God's purpose, encouraging us to recognize God's sovereignty in all things.
7.commentaire: This passage teaches us that even powerful spiritual beings, like angels, are under God's authority and act according to His will. As believers, we must remember that our trust should be placed not in spiritual entities, but in Christ, who is our mediator and Savior. This calls us to live with assurance, knowing that God uses even angels to fulfill His purposes in our lives.

mots.sens: This word means 'throne' and evokes the idea of supreme authority and sovereignty. In the biblical context, it represents royal power and divine majesty. The use of this term to refer to the Son's throne underscores His exalted and eternal position, thus affirming His authority over the universe and His central role in God's plan.

This term translates to 'equity' or 'justice.' It refers to conformity to a divine standard and the establishment of justice in the reign of the Son. The mention of the scepter of His reign as a scepter of equity emphasizes Christ's commitment to govern with justice, which is fundamental to understanding His eternal reign and divine character.

This word means 'eternity' or 'age,' and it evokes the idea of endless time. In this verse, it emphasizes the eternal nature of the Son's throne, affirming that His reign has no beginning or end. This reinforces the understanding of Christ's divinity and His eternal authority in the kingdom of God.

8.epoque: This passage is written in the context of the first century, at a time when Christians faced persecution and doubts regarding the divinity of Christ in relation to Jewish tradition and pagan beliefs.
8.passage: Chapter 1 of Hebrews establishes the superiority of the Son over the angels, affirming His divinity and unique role in the plan of salvation. This verse, quoting Psalm 45, highlights the eternal kingship of Christ.
8.culture: In Jewish culture, the throne is often associated with royalty and messianic promise, while in the Greco-Roman world, the scepter symbolizes authority and power. This duality enriches the understanding of Christ's reign.
8.interpretation: The verse emphasizes that the Son is recognized not only as king but also as God, establishing His divine authority. The eternal throne and the scepter of equity indicate a reign of justice and peace, essential for the Christian faith.
8.commentaire: This verse reminds us that Christ reigns with authority and justice, and that He is our eternal king. As believers, we are called to live under His reign, reflecting His justice in our daily lives. This encourages us to place our trust in Him, knowing that He governs with equity and love.

mots.sens: This word means 'justice' and refers to the state of being just, in accordance with divine standards. It implies moral and ethical rectitude, as well as a correct relationship with God. In this verse, justice is presented as an essential quality of the Messiah, highlighting His perfect character and His role in fulfilling divine will.

This term means 'iniquity' or 'lawlessness,' designating the absence of law or the transgression of divine laws. It evokes a rebellion against the order established by God and a separation from His will. In the context of this verse, the Messiah's hatred of iniquity underscores His commitment to holiness and purity, contrasting with humanity's sins.

This verb means 'to anoint' and is often associated with the idea of consecrating someone for sacred service. In the Old Testament, anointing was a symbolic act marking divine election. Here, the anointing of the Messiah with 'the oil of joy' indicates His divine authority and His role as Savior, bringing joy to those who believe in Him.

This term means 'equality' or 'equity,' indicating a state of balance and justice in relationships. In this verse, it emphasizes that the Messiah is anointed above His equals, highlighting His preeminence and divine authority. This reminds believers of the greatness of Christ as King and Savior.

9.epoque: The book of Hebrews was written in a context where early Christians, primarily of Jewish origin, faced persecution and doubts about the superiority of Christ over the Mosaic law and Jewish traditions.
9.passage: This passage is located in the first chapter of the Epistle to the Hebrews, which establishes the superiority of Christ as the Son of God and Messiah. The author cites passages from the Old Testament to demonstrate that Jesus is the true fulfillment of divine promises.
9.culture: In Jewish culture, anointing was a significant act, often reserved for kings and priests, symbolizing divine selection and approval. This reinforces the idea that the Messiah is the true king and priest, bringing a new covenant.
9.interpretation: This verse emphasizes that love for justice and hatred of iniquity are fundamental characteristics of Christ. His anointing by God with 'the oil of joy' testifies to His divine mission and holy nature, establishing a model for believers.
9.commentaire: This passage reminds us of the importance of seeking justice and fleeing from iniquity in our own lives. By imitating Christ's character, we are called to live in holiness and to testify to the joy that comes from an authentic relationship with God. Let us reflect on our commitment to justice and our attitude toward sin, relying on God's grace to transform us.

mots.sens: This term means 'Lord' and is used to designate a supreme authority. In the biblical context, it is often associated with God's sovereignty over creation. This word emphasizes the divinity of Christ, affirming that He is the creator of all things, which grants Him a unique and supreme position in the plan of salvation.

This word means 'earth' and refers to the physical creation on which we live. In the Bible, the earth is often seen as the place of interaction between God and humanity. The mention of the earth here emphasizes that everything that exists has been established by divine will, reinforcing the idea that God is the creator and sustainer of all things.

This term means 'heavens' and designates the celestial space, the dwelling place of God and celestial beings. In the biblical context, the heavens are often associated with God's glory and authority. The creation of the heavens by the Lord demonstrates His infinite power and His role as the creator of the entire universe.

This word means 'work' or 'deed' and refers to anything produced by labor. In the context of this verse, it evokes the idea that the heavens are the result of God's creative action. This underscores that every aspect of creation is the fruit of divine intention, calling us to recognize the majesty of God's work.

10.epoque: The book of Hebrews was written in a context where early Christians faced persecution and doubts about the superiority of Christ over the Mosaic law and Jewish traditions.
10.passage: This verse is part of an introduction that establishes the superiority of Christ as the Son of God and creator, contrasting with angels and prophets. Chapter 1 of Hebrews emphasizes the divine nature of Christ and His central role in creation.
10.culture: In Jewish culture, creation is a fundamental act that establishes the relationship between God and His people. References to creation in the Old Testament are often used to remind of God's power and faithfulness to His people.
10.interpretation: This verse affirms that Christ, as Lord, is the agent of creation. It reminds us that everything that exists, including ourselves, depends on Him for its existence. Creation is a testimony to His power and authority.
10.commentaire: This passage invites us to recognize the greatness of Christ as creator and Lord. By meditating on creation, we are called to worship the One who made everything and to live in acknowledgment of His sovereignty. It also encourages us to see our place in His divine work and to live according to His will.

mots.sens: This term means 'to perish' or 'to be destroyed.' It evokes a notion of finitude and loss, highlighting the fragility of created things. In the context of this verse, it reminds us that everything material and temporal is destined to disappear, thus reinforcing the permanence of God and His Son, Jesus Christ.

This word means 'to endure' or 'to remain.' It implies a notion of constancy and resilience in the face of time and trials. Spiritually, this underscores the eternal nature of Christ, who remains unshakeable despite the passage of time and the changes of the world.

This term translates to 'garment' and refers to a piece of clothing, symbolizing what is temporary and perishable. In this verse, it is used to illustrate the transient nature of creation compared to the eternity of Christ, thus highlighting the distinction between the material and the spiritual.

11.epoque: The Epistle to the Hebrews was written in a context where Christians faced persecution and doubts about the permanence of their faith, likely between 60 and 70 A.D.
11.passage: This passage is part of an introduction that establishes the superiority of Christ over angels and elements of creation, affirming His divinity and eternal role in God's plan.
11.culture: In the Jewish culture of the time, clothing was often used as a metaphor to represent mortality and the fragility of human existence, contrasting with the majesty and eternity of God.
11.interpretation: This verse reminds us that everything earthly is temporary and destined to disappear, while Christ, as the Son of God, remains eternal. It invites us to place our trust not in material things, but in the One who is constant and unchanging.
11.commentaire: The message of this verse is an encouragement to focus on the eternity and faithfulness of Christ in a constantly changing world. By recognizing that everything around us is perishable, we are called to invest our lives in values and truths that endure. This prompts us to live with an eternal perspective, seeking to glorify God in all that we do.

mots.sens: This word means 'change' or 'transformation.' It evokes the idea of something that is modified or replaced. In the context of this verse, it emphasizes the temporary nature of God's creations compared to the immutability of Christ. This underscores the permanence of Jesus' divinity in the face of the ephemeral nature of creation.

This expression means 'the same.' It emphasizes the uniqueness and immutability of Christ. In the context of this verse, it reminds believers that, despite changes in the world and in creation, Jesus remains constant and faithful, which is a source of comfort and assurance for believers.

The term 'years' refers to a measurable duration of time. In this verse, it emphasizes that Christ's years do not end, contrasting with the ephemeral nature of creation. This highlights the eternal nature of Christ, which is a fundamental pillar of the Christian faith.

12.epoque: The book of Hebrews was written in a first-century context, likely for Jewish Christians facing doubts about the superiority of Christ over the law and Jewish traditions.
12.passage: In chapter 1, the author establishes the superiority of Christ over angels and elements of creation, affirming His divinity and authority. This verse concludes a series of affirmations about the eternal and immutable nature of Jesus.
12.culture: The Jewish culture of the time valued tradition and the immutability of the law. By affirming that Christ is the same and that His years do not end, the author of the epistle underscores the necessity of a faith centered on Christ rather than on passing traditions.
12.interpretation: This verse emphasizes the permanence and faithfulness of Christ in the face of changes in the world. It reminds believers that, although everything around them may change, their Savior remains constant and reliable. This encourages Christians to anchor their faith in Christ, who is eternal.
12.commentaire: This passage reminds us that, in a world of constant change, we have a refuge in Jesus Christ, who never changes. As believers, we are called to rely on this truth and to live with the certainty that our Savior is eternal. This encourages us to persevere in our faith, knowing that we serve a God who remains the same throughout the ages.

mots.sens: This term means 'messengers' and refers to the spiritual beings created by God. In the biblical context, angels are often seen as servants of God, but here, the author of the epistle emphasizes that Jesus, as the Son, holds a superior position to that of the angels, as He has never been called to sit at the right hand of God. The distinction between the Son and the angels is essential for understanding the divinity of Christ and His authority.

This verb means 'to sit' and evokes a position of power and authority. In the context of this verse, it emphasizes that Jesus has been exalted to the right hand of God, a symbol of reign and sovereignty. This sitting at the right hand of God is an affirmation of Christ's victory over His enemies and His role as sovereign in the kingdom of God.

This term designates 'enemies' and refers to those who oppose God and His reign. In the context of this verse, it is emphasized that the enemies of Christ will ultimately be subjected to Him, which testifies to His ultimate victory over evil. This reinforces the idea that Christ is the King who triumphs over all opposition.

This word means 'testimony' or 'evidence.' In the context of the epistle to the Hebrews, it reminds us that Christ's position at the right hand of God is a testimony of His divinity and His salvific role. This underscores the importance of recognizing Jesus not only as a prophet or an angel but as the Son of God who accomplished the work of redemption.

13.epoque: The epistle to the Hebrews was written in a context of persecution of Christians, probably between 60 and 70 A.D., when believers faced pressures to return to traditional Jewish practices.
13.passage: In this passage, the author establishes a comparison between Jesus and the angels, asserting that Jesus has a unique and divine position. Chapter 1 of the epistle to the Hebrews aims to show the superiority of Christ as the Son of God, in contrast to angelic messengers.
13.culture: In the Jewish culture of the time, angels were revered as messengers of God, but the author of the epistle to the Hebrews seeks to redefine this veneration by placing Jesus above all creation, including the angels.
13.interpretation: This verse highlights the majesty and authority of Jesus as the Son of God. By sitting at the right hand of God, He exercises eternal reign and assures victory over His enemies, which is a promise of hope for believers in the face of adversity.
13.commentaire: This passage reminds us that Jesus is not only our Savior but also our King. As Christians, we are called to live in the light of this truth, recognizing His authority over our lives and resting on His promise of victory. This encourages us to persevere in faith, knowing that our struggles are not in vain, for Christ has already triumphed.

mots.sens: The word 'ἄγγελοι' means 'messengers' and refers to spiritual beings created by God. In the biblical context, they are often sent to deliver divine messages or to serve believers. Their role is fundamental in God's plan, as they act as intermediaries between heaven and earth, illustrating how God cares for His people.

The term 'διακονία' translates to 'service' or 'ministry' and evokes the idea of serving with dedication. It is often used in the New Testament to describe the service of the apostles and believers toward God and others. This word emphasizes the importance of humility and self-giving in the Christian life, reflecting the character of Christ who came to serve.

The word 'σωτηρία' means 'salvation' and encompasses the idea of deliverance and spiritual restoration. In the Christian context, it refers to the work of Christ who offers forgiveness of sins and reconciliation with God. This term is central to Christian theology, as it underscores the ultimate purpose of the divine mission and the promised inheritance to believers.

14.epoque: The epistle to the Hebrews was written in a context where early Christians faced persecution and doubts regarding their faith. This historical context underscores the importance of faithfulness and perseverance in faith in Christ.
14.passage: This passage is found in the first chapter of the epistle, which establishes the superiority of Christ over the angels. The author seeks to encourage believers by reminding them that even the angels, though important, are servants of God for the sake of those who inherit salvation.
14.culture: In the Jewish and Greco-Roman culture, angels were often regarded as intermediaries between God and men. Their role was widely recognized, and their presence was perceived as a sign of divine favor.
14.interpretation: This verse emphasizes that angels are not beings to be worshiped, but servants of God, sent to assist believers. This reminds Christians that God cares for them through visible and invisible means, reinforcing their assurance in the salvation they have received.
14.commentaire: This passage reminds us that we are not alone in our walk with God. Angels, as spirits in the service of God, watch over us and assist us in our spiritual journey. By considering their ministry, we are encouraged to live our faith with confidence, knowing that God uses even spiritual beings for our good and salvation.
